The standard practice delivers a MONITORING/INDICATION scheme using vibration probes or oil analysis to detect bearing wear; my same-class mechanism departure is a pure software inference engine that correlates existing motor current signatures with bearing temperature and speed to predict wear progression; the failure-physics connection is that bearing wear increases frictional drag and electrical resistance, which manifests as a measurable shift in the stator current's high-frequency components and a rise in bearing temperature above the normal thermal equilibrium.

PHYSICS CHECK
The governing physical relation is the increase in mechanical loss torque ($\Delta T_{loss}$) due to bearing wear, which increases the electrical power demand ($P_{loss} \approx \Delta T_{loss} \cdot \omega$). This manifests as a shift in the motor current's mean and high-frequency components. DIRECTION-OF-EFFECT: driving variable = bearing frictional torque; the mechanism does not move the driving variable but INFERENCES its trend from electrical signals; this reduces the *probability of undetected failure* by providing a leading indicator that rises before seizure. The magnitude verification is that a 5–10% increase in motor current at constant speed corresponds to a significant increase in frictional losses, detectable well before temperature reaches the 5 bar system's critical limits.
